name: Thingamagoop / Thingamakit
subtitle: Bleep Labs · XR2206 sound chip · 40106 blinkers · TL072 · LM386 amp

keyIdea.eli5: Light plays the pitch. The photocell is a light-controlled faucet for the current that fills the timing bucket: more light fills it faster, and faster means a higher note.
keyIdea.detail: Aim a blinking LEDacle (a bendable LED) at the photocell and light becomes the patch cable between the circuits.

summary: Light sets pitch. The XR2206 makes a triangle or square. A 40106 square can chop it via pin 9. The volume pot and LM386 push it into a tiny speaker.

top.label: +9 V
top.eli5: Red is the + side of the battery: the push every chip drinks from.
top.detail: Each chip has a power pin on this rail. Parts that hang up to it, like the 10k pull-up, borrow its push to set a resting level.

bottom.label: 0 V (ground)
bottom.eli5: Blue is the − side of the battery, and here it is also ground: the floor every voltage is measured from.
bottom.detail: The speaker, both jacks' sleeves, the photocells and the LEDs all come home to this rail.

groundNote.eli5: On the Thingamagoop, ground is the battery's − side (the blue rail). That is the usual setup, called negative ground.

sim.label: Falstad: Schmitt-trigger oscillator (the 40106 blinkers). The XR2206 needs a behavioral stand-in

notes: Pin 9 note: pin 8 isn't drawn on the kit schematic, so a low on pin 9 should starve the oscillator and chop the tone. That is my reading; check it on your board.
The schematic labels the MOD and TRI 40106 gates as pins 10→11 and 8→9. The CD40106 datasheet has inputs 11 and 9 with outputs 10 and 8. The board view follows the datasheet.
The PCB has spots for 20 resistors; the schematic shows 19. The TRI SHAPE pot reads 1M on the schematic and 100k on the PCB silkscreen.

honestyNote.eli5: The sound comes from one Web Audio chain (light → oscillator → wave → volume → amp) plus a side tap for the MOD square. The map and the board show the full branching circuit; the audio engine does not simulate every branch.

job.eli5: Turns light into resistance. That is all a photocell does, and it is enough to play pitch.

wire.eli5: A light-controlled trickle of current, pulled out of XR2206 pin 7.
wire.detail: More light, bigger trickle, higher note.

job.eli5: Fills and empties a tiny bucket (the timing capacitor) over and over, and turns that into a triangle and a square wave.

wire.eli5: The raw tone: a triangle on pin 2 and a square on pin 11.
wire.detail: Both waves exist at once; the WAVEFORM switch picks one.

job.eli5: Picks the triangle or the square, and shrinks the square so both play at a similar volume.

wire.eli5: Whichever wave the switch picked, still riding on the chip's steady resting voltage.

job.eli5: A door blocks the steady push, then the volume knob picks how much sound goes on.

wire.eli5: The tone, shrunk by the volume knob. The Out jack listens to this same wire.

job.eli5: A small muscle (power amp) shoves a small speaker: no deep bass, a little grit.

wire.eli5: Big swings of current that push and pull the speaker cone.

job.eli5: The battery is the water tower, and the switch on the volume knob is the main valve.
Three slow blinkers make LEDacle 1 flicker. They only make light.
A metronome square that can chop the tone (patch B) or blink the LED (patch A).

wire.eli5: A slow on/off square heading to node B (pin 9) or to LEDacle 1.

job.eli5: A third slow square, smoothed by an op-amp into a breathing glow for LEDacle 2. Light only.
The water tower: it holds the push (voltage) that every part spends.
job.detail: Its + side feeds the +9 V rail through the power switch. Its − side is ground.

order.eli5: It sits off the board on two wires, because you have to swap it out.
order.detail: The wires land on the BAT pads at the board's right edge.

breaks.eli5: No battery, no push: everything goes dark and silent.
breaks.detail: A tired battery first makes the pitch drift and the amp crackle.

parts.label: Power switch (on the back of the volume pot)

job.eli5: The main valve: turn the volume knob past its click and the battery's push flows in.
job.detail: The switch is built into the volume pot, so 'off' and 'quietest' share one knob.

order.eli5: It sits between the battery's + side and the +9 V rail, so it cuts everything at once.

breaks.eli5: No path for the battery: no power. Bridge it and the toy stays on forever.

job.eli5: A little water tank next to the chip, so it never goes thirsty when the amp gulps current.
job.detail: It sits from the +9 V pin to ground and fills in quick dips in the supply.

order.eli5: Right beside the chip's power pin. A long wire would make the tank too far away to help.

breaks.eli5: The amp's gulps make the supply wobble, and the pitch warbles with a putt-putt sound (motorboating).

job.eli5: A light-controlled faucet: more light lets more current through.
job.detail: It is the XR2206's timing resistor, from pin 7 to ground. More current fills the timing cap faster, so the pitch goes up.

order.eli5: It hangs off pin 7, the chip's 'how fast?' input, so it decides the pitch before you hear anything.
order.detail: It sits off the board on two wires so it can poke out of the face.

breaks.eli5: Shut the faucet and the oscillator stops: silence.
breaks.detail: Swap in a fixed resistor and you get one fixed pitch.

tune.higher: A darker-rated photocell (more ohms in the same light): the faucet is tighter, so the bucket fills slower and the pitch drops.
tune.lower: A lower-ohm photocell: a wider faucet, so the pitch climbs.
tune.tooFar: The XR2206 wants its timing resistor between 1k and 2M (best between 4k and 200k). Below 1k it pulls too much current; the datasheet caps the timing current at 3 mA.

job.eli5: The bucket the photocell fills: a big bucket fills slowly (low notes), a small one fills fast (high notes).
job.detail: The .01 µF cap always sits across pins 5 and 6. The RANGE switch adds the .1 µF beside it for the low range.

order.eli5: It sits right on the chip's timing pins, because faucet and bucket together set the pitch.

breaks.eli5: No bucket, nothing to fill and empty, so no oscillation.

tune.higher: Bigger timing cap: a bigger bucket takes longer to fill, so the pitch drops.
tune.lower: Smaller: it fills in a blink and squeaks higher.
tune.tooFar: Huge (10 µF) and the pitch slows into clicks; tiny (1 nF) and it sings above your hearing. The datasheet recommends 1 nF to 100 µF.

lugs.eli5: A toggle is a railroad junction: the middle lug is the track you're on, and the bat picks which side track it joins.
lugs.detail: This is an SPDT (single pole, double throw) switch: one common lug, two throws.
lugs.standard: Standard part: a mini toggle switch (SPDT, on-on).

lugs.name: throw
lugs.eli5: To the extra .1 µF timing cap.

lugs.name: common
lugs.eli5: Timing cap node (pin 6).

lugs.name: throw
lugs.eli5: Unused.

parts.label: XR2206 function generator
parts.term: function generator IC (integrated circuit: a chip)

job.eli5: The heart: it fills and empties the timing bucket over and over and turns that into a triangle and a square.
job.detail: Pin 2 gives the triangle, pin 11 the square. Pins 13 and 14 stay open, so the triangle stays a triangle instead of being rounded into a sine.

order.eli5: It sits in the middle: everything before it sets its speed, everything after it shapes and amplifies it.

breaks.eli5: No heart, no sound at all.

use.7: Photocell 1 is the timing faucet here, so light sets the pitch.
use.5: One side of the timing caps (RANGE switch).
use.6: The other side of the timing caps.
use.13: Left open, so the chip makes a triangle.
use.14: Left open, so the chip makes a triangle.
use.9: The MOD patch can chop this pin (node B).

job.eli5: Two equal resistors split the battery in half, like a seesaw balanced in the middle, and pin 3 sits on that middle.
job.detail: Pin 3 sets the output level and centers the wave, so it has equal room to swing up and down.

order.eli5: One resistor goes up to the + rail, one down to ground, and the middle feeds pin 3.

breaks.eli5: The seesaw tips: the output goes very quiet or lopsided.

tune.higher: Bigger divider resistors: the same half-way point, a little less current from the battery.
tune.lower: Smaller: the same half-way point, more current wasted.
tune.tooFar: Unequal pairs move pin 3 off center and the wave clips on one side.
tune.real: You would hear this on the real board only if the two resistors differ (lopsided clipping). This sketch does not model it.

parts.label: Pin 10 bypass cap

job.eli5: A shock absorber on the chip's internal reference, so tiny ripples don't wiggle the pitch.
job.detail: Pin 10 holds the XR2206's own reference voltage. The datasheet asks for a cap from here to ground.

order.eli5: Straight from pin 10 to ground, on the shortest path the board allows.

breaks.eli5: The reference picks up noise, so the tone gets less steady.

parts.silentNote: The model has no internal reference to disturb, so you won't hear this one.

tune.higher: Bigger bias cap: a calmer reference and less hiss.
tune.lower: Smaller: more supply noise leaks into the tone.
tune.tooFar: Leave it out and the reference wobbles with the battery.
tune.real: You would hear this on the real board as more or less hum and hiss. This sketch does not model it.

parts.label: Node B (pin 9)
parts.term: FSK input (frequency-shift keying: a pin that flips between two timing settings)

job.eli5: A remote on/off button for the oscillator, pressed by the MOD square.
job.detail: Pin 9 picks which timing pin (7 or 8) runs the chip. Pin 8 has nothing on it, so a low on pin 9 starves the oscillator and the tone chops. That is my reading of the schematic; check it on your board.

order.eli5: It comes in from the side chain (the helper circuits), not from the audio path.

breaks.eli5: Nobody presses the button: a steady, unchopped tone.

job.eli5: A spring that pulls the square back up, because pin 11 can only pull down by itself.
job.detail: Pin 11 is an open-collector output: it can only connect to ground or let go. The resistor gives it a high level to return to.

order.eli5: It hangs from the + rail straight onto pin 11.

breaks.eli5: The square has no 'up', so square mode goes silent.

tune.higher: Bigger pull-up: a weaker lift, so the square's rising edge rounds off and gets quieter.
tune.lower: Smaller: a crisper, louder square, and more current from the battery.
tune.tooFar: Below about 1k the chip strains to pull it down; very big and the square turns into a shark fin.
tune.real: You would hear this on the real board as a rounder or crisper square wave. This sketch does not model it.

job.eli5: Shrinks the big square to the triangle's size, so flipping the switch doesn't jump in volume.
job.detail: With the 10k pull-up, the first 750 Ω keeps only a thin slice of the 9 V swing. The second 750 Ω gives the switch output a path to ground.

order.eli5: Between the square output and the WAVEFORM switch.

breaks.eli5: Square mode blasts much louder than triangle mode.

tune.higher: Bigger: the square comes out quieter next to the triangle.
tune.lower: Smaller: the square comes out louder.
tune.tooFar: Very small and the square drowns the triangle when you flip the switch.
tune.real: On the real board these only change the square; the sketch turns the whole switch output up or down.

parts.label: Waveform switch
parts.term: SPDT toggle (single pole, double throw: one input, two choices)

job.eli5: A railroad switch: it sends either the triangle or the square down the track.
job.detail: Triangle comes from pin 2, square from pin 11.

order.eli5: After both waves exist and before the shared volume path.

breaks.eli5: Stuck on one waveform.

lugs.eli5: A toggle is a railroad junction: the middle lug is the track you're on, and the bat picks which side track it joins.
lugs.detail: This is an SPDT (single pole, double throw) switch: one common lug, two throws.
lugs.standard: Standard part: a mini toggle switch (SPDT, on-on).

lugs.name: throw (square)
lugs.eli5: Pin 11's square wave.

lugs.name: common
lugs.eli5: Out to the volume pot.

lugs.name: throw (triangle)
lugs.eli5: Pin 2's triangle wave.

parts.label: Output coupling cap

job.eli5: A door that lets the wiggles through but blocks the steady push.
job.detail: The XR2206 output rides on a few volts of steady DC (direct current, the part that doesn't wiggle). The cap passes only the audio.

order.eli5: Between the chip and the volume pot, so the pot never carries the steady push.

breaks.eli5: Steady push leaks into the pot and amp: a scratchy knob and earlier distortion.

parts.silentNote: The steady push makes no sound on its own, so the model can't show this. On the real board you'd hear a scratchy pot and earlier distortion.

tune.higher: Bigger output cap: more bass reaches the jack.
tune.lower: Smaller: the bass gets cut and it sounds thin.
tune.tooFar: Around 10 nF the low pitches nearly vanish through the jack.
tune.real: You would hear this on the real board as more or less bass at the out jack. This sketch does not model it.

job.eli5: A slider on a ramp: the middle pin (the wiper) picks how much of the sound to keep.
job.detail: Signal goes in on lug 3, lug 1 goes to ground, and the wiper feeds both the LM386 and the Out jack.

order.eli5: Before the power amp, so it sets the level without touching the oscillator.

breaks.eli5: Always full volume.

lugs.eli5: A pot with a power switch on its back: turn it up from zero and it clicks the battery on.
lugs.detail: Use all three lugs and it is a voltage divider (a volume knob). Use one end and the wiper and it is a variable resistor (a faucet).
lugs.standard: Standard part: a potentiometer (A = log taper for volume, B = linear).

lugs.name: end 1
lugs.eli5: One end of the resistive track.

lugs.name: wiper
lugs.eli5: The middle lug rides along the track as you turn: it sends some of the tone to the amp and jack.

lugs.name: end 3
lugs.eli5: The other end of the track.

lugs.name: switch
lugs.eli5: Battery + comes in.

lugs.name: switch
lugs.eli5: The +9 V rail, live once the switch clicks on.

parts.label: Out jack (¼ inch)

job.eli5: A side door for the sound: plug in a cable to send the tone to an amp or recorder.
job.detail: It taps the volume pot's wiper beside the LM386, so it skips the little amp and speaker.

order.eli5: It branches off after the volume knob, next to the amp rather than after it.

breaks.eli5: No line out. The speaker still plays.

parts.silentNote: The model always listens at the speaker path, so pulling this jack changes nothing you hear.

job.eli5: A muscle: it turns a small signal into enough current to shove a speaker cone.
job.detail: Its gain pins (1 and 8) stay open, which gives the chip's lowest built-in boost.

order.eli5: Last of the active parts, because a power amp works on the finished sound.

breaks.eli5: The speaker goes silent. The Out jack still works.

use.1: Open: no gain cap, so the gain is 20.

job.eli5: A big door that passes the speaker's wiggles but blocks the amp's steady half-battery push.
job.detail: The LM386 output rests at half the supply. Without this cap that steady voltage would sit on the speaker coil.

order.eli5: Between the amp and the speaker. It has to be big to pass bass into a speaker's low resistance.

breaks.eli5: The steady push holds the cone out, drains the battery, and distorts.
breaks.detail: A smaller cap here loses bass.

tune.higher: Bigger speaker cap: more bass reaches the little speaker.
tune.lower: Smaller: the bass is cut and it gets thin and buzzy.
tune.tooFar: Very small (10 µF) and a speaker this size plays almost no lows; the cap also protects the speaker from DC, so never leave it out.

job.eli5: A paper drum moved by a magnet: current in, air movement out.
job.detail: A small cone can't push enough air for deep bass.

order.eli5: The end of the line, off the board on two wires.

breaks.eli5: Quiet. Only the Out jack plays.

parts.label: 3 blink oscillators (1M / 1.5M / 10M)

job.eli5: Three slow blinkers at different speeds, like three people tapping out of sync.
job.detail: Each 40106 gate has a resistor from its output back to its input and a .1 µF cap to ground. The cap fills until the gate flips, then empties until it flips back.

order.eli5: They live in the side chain: they make light, not sound.

breaks.eli5: LEDacle 1 stops flickering.

parts.silentNote: These only make light. Set 'LEDacle → photocell' to Aimed to hear light become modulation.

use.13: Gate F's unused input, tied to ground so it can't float.

parts.label: Blink mixing resistors

job.eli5: Three blinkers pour into one cup through separate straws, so none of them drowns out the others.
job.detail: Each blinker goes through 220 Ω to node A. One more 220 Ω keeps the LED's current safe.

order.eli5: Between the blinkers and LEDacle 1.

breaks.eli5: The outputs fight each other and the LED gets too much current.

parts.silentNote: Light only. The model doesn't simulate LED brightness.

tune.higher: Bigger LED resistors: dimmer LEDacles and a calmer battery.
tune.lower: Smaller: brighter LEDs, until the 40106's outputs can't keep up.
tune.tooFar: Too small and you ask more of the chip and LED than they like; keep LED current under about 20 mA.
tune.real: Silent in this sketch. On the real board brighter LEDs push more light into the photocell.

job.eli5: A bendable flashlight you can aim at a photocell: an optical patch cable.

order.eli5: The end of the light side chain, off the board on two wires.

breaks.eli5: No optical modulation.

job.eli5: A metronome: a steady on/off square that can chop the tone or blink the LED.
job.detail: Another 40106 gate with a speed resistor from output to input and a cap to ground.

order.eli5: Side chain. The MOD PATCH switch sends its square to A (LEDs) or B (pin 9).

breaks.eli5: No rhythmic chopping.

parts.label: MOD rate pot
parts.term: pot wired as a variable resistor (rheostat)

job.eli5: The metronome's speed knob: less resistance fills the cap faster, so the ticks come faster.

order.eli5: In the feedback path from the gate's output back to its input.

breaks.eli5: No feedback path, so the metronome stops (unless Photocell 2 is selected).

tune.higher: Bigger MOD rate pot: a tighter faucet at full turn, so the chop can go much slower.
tune.lower: Smaller: the slowest setting is still fast.
tune.tooFar: Very big and the slow end crawls to a stop.

sections.title: Power
sections.eli5: The battery and its valve. Every chip drinks from the red rail and returns to the blue one.

honesty.eli5: Not modeled. The app's battery never runs down.
honesty.detail: A real tired battery makes the pitch drift and the LM386 crackle early.

sections.title: Sound oscillator (XR2206)
sections.eli5: Where the tone is born: light sets the speed, the chip makes the wave.

honesty.eli5: Modeled by behavior: a Web Audio oscillator whose pitch follows your light slider.
honesty.detail: The real triangle is slightly rounded, and the light-to-pitch curve depends on your exact photocell. The model uses one smooth curve.

sections.title: LED + MOD oscillators (40106)
sections.eli5: Four slow blinkers on one chip: three flicker LEDacle 1, one (MOD) can chop the tone.

honesty.eli5: Approximated. The MOD square that chops the tone is modeled. The three LED blinkers only appear as a wobble when you set the LEDacle to 'aimed'.
honesty.detail: Real light from an LED onto a photocell is uneven and slow; the model uses a simple wobble.

sections.title: TRI shaper (TL072)
sections.eli5: Turns the TRI square into a breathing glow for LEDacle 2.

honesty.eli5: Not modeled. It only makes light, and the app doesn't simulate LEDacle 2 shining on a photocell.

sections.title: Volume + LM386 amp
sections.eli5: The volume knob, then a small muscle that pushes the speaker.

honesty.eli5: Approximated: a volume stage plus a speaker-shaped filter (no deep bass, a little grit).
honesty.detail: The real LM386 clips harder as the battery sags, and the real speaker rattles in its box.

sections.title: Photocell 2
sections.eli5: The MOD speed eye (via MOD SEL).

sections.title: Out jack
sections.eli5: The side door for a cable.

links.label: light → pin 7
links.eli5: Light in, current out: the photocell decides how fast the timing bucket fills.
links.detail: This is a control signal: it never carries the sound, it sets the speed of the thing that makes the sound.

links.label: triangle or square
links.eli5: The finished tone travels to the volume knob.
links.detail: Through the .1 µF door, so only the wiggles arrive.

links.label: LM386 → 220 µF → speaker
links.eli5: Big current wiggles go out to push the cone.

links.label: volume wiper → Out (parallel branch)
links.eli5: A second exit: the Out jack listens to the volume knob directly, side by side with the amp.
links.detail: This is a branch: one wire, two destinations at once.

links.label: MOD square → node B → pin 9
links.eli5: An on/off finger on the oscillator's remote button: patched to B, it chops the tone.
links.detail: Only when MOD PATCH is on B.

links.label: blinkers (+ MOD on A) → LEDacle 1
links.eli5: Three blinkers, plus the MOD square when patched to A, pour into LEDacle 1.

links.label: light → MOD speed
links.eli5: Light on Photocell 2 can set the metronome speed instead of the knob.
links.detail: Only when MOD SEL picks the photocell.

links.label: TRI square → .33 µF → TL072
links.eli5: The 40106's third metronome hands its square to the op-amp to be smoothed.

links.label: breathing wave → LEDacle 2
links.eli5: The smoothed wave sets how bright LEDacle 2 glows.

links.label: light, if you aim it
links.eli5: Bend LEDacle 1 toward Photocell 1 and the blinks wobble the pitch. Light is the patch cable.
links.detail: The only way the blinkers ever reach the sound.

links.label: light, if you aim it
links.eli5: Same trick with the breathing LEDacle: a slow swoop in pitch.

links.label: +9 V / ground
links.eli5: Pin 4 drinks from the red rail; pins 1 and 12 return to ground.

board.fidelityNote: Part placement follows the real Thingamakit PCB (Bleep Labs assembly guide, pages 2 and 4): four toggles on top, DIP sockets in the middle, three resistor banks, ceramic cap columns, three board-mounted pots, wire pads on the right edge. The copper traces are redrawn from the schematic, not traced from the kit. The guide's photos don't show the routing.

nets.name: Ground (0 V)
nets.eli5: Ground: the shared floor. Every signal comes back here to finish its loop.
nets.detail: On the kit it is a wide copper area (a ground pour) instead of thin traces, so every part has a short, quiet way home.

nets.name: +9 V rail
nets.eli5: The red rail: the battery's push, delivered to every chip's power pin.
nets.detail: It only exists while the power switch on the volume knob is on.

nets.name: Battery + (before switch)
nets.eli5: The battery's + side, waiting at the power switch.
nets.detail: Turn the volume knob past its click and this joins the +9 V rail.

nets.name: Pin 7 · timing current
nets.eli5: A light-controlled trickle of current out of pin 7, through Photocell 1, to ground.
nets.detail: The chip copies this current to fill the timing bucket. More light, bigger trickle, higher note.

nets.name: Timing cap A (pin 5)
nets.eli5: One side of the timing bucket. A ramp goes up and down here as the chip fills and empties it.

nets.name: Timing cap B (pin 6)
nets.eli5: The other side of the timing bucket.

nets.name: RANGE switch → .1 µF
nets.eli5: When RANGE closes, the big .1 µF bucket joins the small one, and the pitch drops.

nets.name: Pin 3 · half voltage
nets.eli5: The seesaw's middle: about 4.5 V, half the battery.
nets.detail: Pin 3 uses it to center the output wave.

nets.name: Pin 10 · reference
nets.eli5: The chip's internal reference, steadied by a 1 µF shock absorber.

nets.name: Pin 2 · triangle out
nets.eli5: The triangle wave, on its way to the WAVEFORM switch.

nets.name: Pin 11 · square out
nets.eli5: The square wave: the pull-up lifts it, the 750 Ω shrinks it.

nets.name: Switch out
nets.eli5: Whichever wave the switch picked, still riding on the chip's steady push.

nets.name: To volume pot
nets.eli5: Pure wiggles now: the .1 µF door kept the steady push behind.

nets.name: Volume wiper → LM386 + Out
nets.eli5: The sound after the volume knob. It splits here: one copy to the LM386, one to the Out jack.
nets.detail: That split is a parallel branch, not a chain.

nets.name: LM386 out
nets.eli5: The amp's output: big current wiggles riding on half the battery voltage.

nets.name: To speaker
nets.eli5: Only the wiggles, now strong enough to push the cone.

nets.name: Blinker 1 timing
nets.eli5: Blinker 1's bucket fills and empties through the 1M resistor.

nets.name: Blinker 1 out
nets.eli5: Blinker 1's on/off square.

nets.name: Blinker 2 timing
nets.eli5: Blinker 2's bucket (1.5M: a bit slower).

nets.name: Blinker 2 out
nets.eli5: Blinker 2's on/off square.

nets.name: Blinker 3 timing
nets.eli5: Blinker 3's bucket (10M: very slow).

nets.name: Blinker 3 out
nets.eli5: Blinker 3's on/off square.

nets.name: Node A
nets.eli5: The cup where the blinkers mix (plus the MOD square on patch A).
nets.detail: The mix flickers in an uneven, organic way because the three speeds never line up.

nets.name: To LEDacle 1
nets.eli5: Current for LEDacle 1, limited by 220 Ω.

nets.name: MOD timing
nets.eli5: The MOD metronome's bucket and its two possible speed controls.

nets.name: MOD range .33 µF
nets.eli5: The small (fast) MOD bucket.

nets.name: MOD range 1 µF
nets.eli5: The big (slow) MOD bucket.

nets.name: MOD SEL ← rate pot
nets.eli5: The rate pot's path back to the gate's output.

nets.name: MOD SEL ← Photocell 2
nets.eli5: Photocell 2's path back to the gate's output.

nets.name: MOD square out
nets.eli5: The MOD metronome's on/off square, on its way to the MOD PATCH switch.

nets.name: Patch A → node A
nets.eli5: Patch A: the MOD square joins the blinkers.

nets.name: Node B → pin 9
nets.eli5: Patch B: the MOD square presses the oscillator's on/off button.
nets.detail: When it goes low, the tone stops; when high, it plays. That is the chop.

nets.name: TRI timing
nets.eli5: The TRI metronome's bucket and speed knob.

nets.name: TRI rate → 220 Ω
nets.eli5: The speed path, with a 220 Ω so the knob at zero can't short the gate.

nets.name: TRI square out
nets.eli5: The TRI metronome's square, heading to the op-amp.

nets.name: TL072 input
nets.eli5: Only the square's edges get through the .33 µF door.

nets.name: TL072 minus input
nets.eli5: Where input and feedback meet: the op-amp works to keep this point steady.

nets.name: TL072 out
nets.eli5: The breathing wave, ready to light LEDacle 2.

nets.name: To LEDacle 2
nets.eli5: Current for LEDacle 2, limited by 220 Ω.

nets.name: TL072 plus input
nets.eli5: The TRI SHAPE wiper sets this resting level, sliding the breathing up or down.

nets.name: TRI SHAPE top
nets.eli5: Top of the shape divider, fed from +9 V through 30k.

nets.name: TRI SHAPE bottom
nets.eli5: Bottom of the shape divider, to ground through 30k.
